title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
text:
Few developments have reshaped global society as profoundly as the rapid maturation of artificial intelligence. Proponents argue that automation could unlock unprecedented productivity, freeing humans from repetitive labour and enabling them to pursue more creative endeavours. Critics, however, caution that the benefits are unlikely to be distributed evenly, and that entire professions may be rendered obsolete faster than societies can retrain their workforces. The resulting tension is less a purely technical question than a deeply political one.

Ethical considerations complicate the picture further. Algorithms trained on historical data can quietly entrench the prejudices embedded in that data, producing decisions that appear objective while reproducing old inequities. Consequently, many scholars advocate for transparency requirements and independent auditing before such systems are deployed in sensitive domains such as lending or criminal justice. Whether these safeguards will prove adequate remains an open question.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what do critics worry about?
options: They think the benefits of automation will be shared evenly.
Entire professions may disappear faster than workers can be retrained.
Artificial intelligence will stop improving soon.
Humans will lose the ability to do creative work.

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, why do many scholars call for transparency and auditing?
options: Algorithms are too expensive to build.
Algorithms trained on historical data can repeat existing prejudices.
Lending decisions are never made by humans.
Criminal justice does not use any technology.

questions.text: What can the reader infer about the author's view of the debate over artificial intelligence?
options: It is mainly a technical problem that is easy to solve.
It involves political and social choices as well as technology.
Automation will have no real effect on workers.
Existing safeguards are certain to be sufficient.

questions.text: What can the reader infer about decisions that appear objective, as described in the second paragraph?
options: They are always fair because they are based on data.
They may look neutral while carrying hidden bias.
They cannot be produced by any algorithm.
They are only used in lending and never elsewhere.

paragraph_translations: Poucos desenvolvimentos remodelaram a sociedade global tão profundamente quanto a rápida maturação da inteligência artificial. Defensores argumentam que a automação poderia desbloquear uma produtividade sem precedentes, libertando os seres humanos do trabalho repetitivo e permitindo que se dediquem a empreendimentos mais criativos. Críticos, porém, advertem que é improvável que os benefícios sejam distribuídos de forma equitativa, e que profissões inteiras poderão tornar-se obsoletas mais depressa do que as sociedades conseguem requalificar a sua força de trabalho. A tensão resultante é menos uma questão puramente técnica do que uma questão profundamente política.

As considerações éticas complicam ainda mais o quadro. Algoritmos treinados com dados históricos podem, discretamente, enraizar os preconceitos incorporados nesses dados, produzindo decisões que parecem objetivas enquanto reproduzem antigas desigualdades. Consequentemente, muitos investigadores defendem requisitos de transparência e auditorias independentes antes de tais sistemas serem implementados em áreas sensíveis, como o crédito ou a justiça criminal. Se essas salvaguardas se revelarão adequadas continua a ser uma questão em aberto.
